files.lesson.md: --- order: 6 unit: angle-sums node: AC9M7M05 n3 assumes: [AC9M6M04 n1, AC9M6M04 n2] uses: [AC9M7M04 n3] # chains of reasons with parallel-line angles (Reasoning with angles) title: Unknown angles in shapes summary: "Find unknown angles in triangles and polygons in steps, with a reason for each: the angle sum of the shape, angles on a straight line, equal angles in an isosceles triangle. An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A roof truss, a kite, a bridge brace: builders work out the angle they cannot measure from the ones they can. Every step needs a reason." connection: rafter-cut app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8172 url: http://127.0.0.1:8172/index.html readySelector: "#kmove-pt" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: shapes.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$a = 59^\\circ$, $b = 45^\\circ$. Then $c = 76^\\circ$ (angles in a triangle add to $180^\\circ$) and $x = 104^\\circ$ ($c$ and $x$ are on a straight line). And $x = a + b$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@shapes.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "From the angle sum to the exterior angle" say: "Two reasons find any angle here." clip: - caption: { text: "a + b + c = 180°: the angles in a triangle.", say: "The angles in a triangle add to one hundred and eighty degrees." } - wait: 900 - caption: { text: "x and c make a straight line: x = 180° − c.", say: "x and c make a straight line, so x is one eighty take c." } - wait: 900 - caption: { text: "So x = a + b, whatever the shape.", say: "So x is always a plus b. Watch it as the triangle changes." } - click: Move A right - click: Move A right - click: Move A up - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "= 180°" } - wait: 1200 --- You know the angle sums: a triangle's angles add to $180^\circ$, and a polygon with $n$ sides has $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$. With straight-line angles and the parallel-line rules, you can find angles you cannot measure. As in Reasoning with angles, each step needs a reason. Write your working your own way; the checker marks your answer and a reason at the key step, then shows a model to compare. ## Predict: the outside angle ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the exterior angle before working it out shows whether they see the two-step chain (angle sum, then straight line), and sets up x = a + b." check: type: predict q: "A triangle has $a = 50^\\circ$ and $b = 60^\\circ$. The side through $C$ is extended past $C$, making an outside angle $x$ with the third side. What is $x$?" options: - "$110^\\circ$" - "$70^\\circ$" - "$130^\\circ$" - "$120^\\circ$" actual: "110°. c = 180° − 50° − 60° = 70° (angles in a triangle), then x = 180° − 70° = 110° (a straight line). Notice: 110° = 50° + 60°." ``` Two steps: which angle can you find first? ## Run: drag the triangle ```step stage: run insight: "Dragging the triangle while watching x shows the exterior angle always equals the two opposite angles added: the two-step chain gives a shortcut." try: { playground: board, starter: "shapes.yml#run", height: 600 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag the corners (or use Move) until $x$ is more than $120^\\circ$. Each time, compare $x$ with $a + b$.", when: "x > 120" } ``` Was your prediction right? Is $x$ always $a + b$? Why must it be? ## Investigate: angle sums in steps ```step stage: investigate insight: "Choose the angle sum for the shape, then any straight-line or parallel-line step, with a reason each time. Zoe's mistake uses the triangle's 180° for a quadrilateral." tasks: - picture: { ref: shapes.yml#tri1, caption: "$a = 59^\\circ$, $b = 45^\\circ$. The side $BC$ is extended past $C$." } check: type: reasoning q: "Find $x$. Write each step with its reason." steps: - ["$c = 180^\\circ - 59^\\circ - 45^\\circ = 76^\\circ$", "angles in a triangle add to $180^\\circ$"] - ["$x = 180^\\circ - 76^\\circ = 104^\\circ$", "$c$ and $x$ are on a straight line"] picks: - step: 1 options: ["Angles in a triangle add to 180°", "Angles on a straight line add to 180°", "Angles at a point add to 360°"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "a, b and c are the corners of a triangle, not on one line.", "a, b and c are not around one point."] answer: "104" feedback: - ["76", "That is c. One more step: c and x are on a straight line."] explain: "c = 76° (angles in a triangle), x = 104° (a straight line with c). Check: 59° + 45° = 104°." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#zoe" text: "Zoe finds the fourth angle of a quadrilateral. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: wrong-angle-sum explain: "Line 2: a quadrilateral's angles add to (4 − 2) × 180° = 360°, not 180°. d = 360° − 76° − 68° − 102° = 114°. A negative angle on line 4 is the clue that something earlier went wrong." - picture: { ref: shapes.yml#quad1, caption: "A quadrilateral: $a = 76^\\circ$, $b = 68^\\circ$, $c = 102^\\circ$." } check: type: reasoning q: "Find $d$, with your reason." steps: - ["$a + b + c + d = 360^\\circ$", "angles in a quadrilateral: $(4 - 2) \\times 180^\\circ$"] - ["$d = 360^\\circ - 76^\\circ - 68^\\circ - 102^\\circ = 114^\\circ$", "subtract the angles you know"] picks: - step: 1 options: ["The angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°", "The angles of a quadrilateral add to 180°", "The angles of a quadrilateral add to 540°"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "180° is a triangle. A quadrilateral splits into 2 triangles.", "540° is a pentagon: (5 − 2) × 180°."] answer: "114" feedback: - ["-66", "A negative angle: the sum must be bigger than 180°."] explain: "(4 − 2) × 180° = 360°, so d = 360° − 246° = 114°." ``` ### Triangle, then a straight line Here is the routine: know, choose the rule, say why. ```worked a = 59^\circ,\; b = 45^\circ :: Know: the given angles. c = 180^\circ - 59^\circ - 45^\circ = 76^\circ :: Choose: $a$, $b$, $c$ are a triangle's angles. Why: angles in a triangle add to $180^\circ$. x = 180^\circ - 76^\circ = 104^\circ :: Choose: $c$ and $x$ sit on one straight line. Why: angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$. x = 59^\circ + 45^\circ :: A shortcut you can now explain: an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. ``` Now find $x$ yourself, your own way. ### Find the mistake Read Zoe's working. Which line uses the wrong fact? ### A quadrilateral ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: an isosceles triangle, a pentagon's sum, the exterior angle at another corner, a right angle in a quadrilateral, then the edge case of a triangle that cannot exist." try: { playground: board, starter: "shapes.yml#make", height: 600 } tasks: - picture: { ref: shapes.yml#iso, caption: "$CA = CB$ (isosceles). $a = 56^\\circ$." } check: type: reasoning q: "$CA = CB$, so the angles at $A$ and $B$ are equal. Find $c$, with a reason for each step." steps: - ["$b = 56^\\circ$", "isosceles triangle: the angles opposite the equal sides are equal"] - ["$c = 180^\\circ - 56^\\circ - 56^\\circ = 68^\\circ$", "angles in a triangle add to $180^\\circ$"] picks: - step: 2 options: ["Angles in a triangle add to 180°", "Angles on a straight line add to 180°", "Vertically opposite angles are equal"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "a, b and c are a triangle's corners, not on one line.", "There is no crossing here."] answer: "68" feedback: - ["124", "That is 180° − 56°: you need to take away both 56° angles."] explain: "b = 56° (isosceles), c = 68° (angles in a triangle)." - picture: { ref: shapes.yml#pent, caption: "A pentagon: $a = 104^\\circ$, $b = 117^\\circ$, $c = 85^\\circ$, $d = 136^\\circ$." } check: type: answer q: "Find $e$." answer: "98" feedback: - ["-82", "A pentagon's angles add to (5 − 2) × 180° = 540°."] - ["-262", "A pentagon's angles add to 540°, not 180°."] explain: "(5 − 2) × 180° = 540°, so e = 540° − 442° = 98°." - picture: { ref: shapes.yml#ext-b, caption: "$a = 63^\\circ$, $c = 87^\\circ$. The side $AB$ is extended past $B$." } check: type: reasoning q: "Find the exterior angle $x$ at $B$." steps: - ["$b = 180^\\circ - 63^\\circ - 87^\\circ = 30^\\circ$", "angles in a triangle add to $180^\\circ$"] - ["$x = 180^\\circ - 30^\\circ = 150^\\circ$", "$b$ and $x$ are on a straight line"] answer: "150" feedback: - ["30", "That is b. One more step to x."] explain: "b = 30°, x = 150°. Or straight away: x = a + c = 63° + 87° = 150° (the exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles)." - picture: { ref: shapes.yml#quad2, caption: "A quadrilateral with a right angle at $B$: $a = 68^\\circ$, $d = 102^\\circ$." } check: type: answer q: "Find $c$." answer: "100" feedback: - ["-80", "A quadrilateral's angles add to 360°."] - ["10", "Include the right angle at B: 90°."] explain: "360° − 68° − 90° − 102° = 100°." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: can a triangle have two angles of $100^\\circ$?" options: ["No: they already add to more than 180°", "Yes, if the third angle is small", "Yes, if the triangle is big enough"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "100° + 100° = 200°, which is already more than 180°.", "Size does not change angles: every triangle's add to 180°."] explain: "100° + 100° = 200° > 180°, so no. A triangle has at most one obtuse angle." ``` ### Isosceles Each task changes one thing. ### A pentagon ### Exterior at another corner ### A right angle ### Impossible triangles ## Practise: unknown angles ```step stage: practise insight: "Angle sums and exterior angles from words, mixed, with the polygon sum planted; the review keeps the parallel-line chains fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A triangle has angles of $35^\\circ$ and $85^\\circ$. Find the third angle." answer: "60" feedback: - ["240", "Add the two angles, then take that from 180°."] explain: "180° − 35° − 85° = 60°." - check: type: answer q: "Three angles of a quadrilateral are $90^\\circ$, $85^\\circ$ and $120^\\circ$. Find the fourth." answer: "65" feedback: - ["-115", "A quadrilateral's angles add to 360°, not 180°."] explain: "360° − 295° = 65°." - check: type: reasoning q: "A triangle has an exterior angle of $130^\\circ$ at $C$, and $a = 70^\\circ$. Find $b$, with your reasons." steps: - ["$c = 180^\\circ - 130^\\circ = 50^\\circ$", "$c$ and the exterior angle are on a straight line"] - ["$b = 180^\\circ - 70^\\circ - 50^\\circ = 60^\\circ$", "angles in a triangle add to $180^\\circ$"] answer: "60" feedback: - ["50", "That is c. Now use the triangle."] explain: "c = 50°, b = 60°. Or: 130° = a + b, so b = 60°." - check: type: question q: "Review: parallel lines, $c = 70^\\circ$. Which is a correct first step to find $e$?" options: ["$e = 110^\\circ$: co-interior with $c$", "$e = 70^\\circ$: alternate to $c$", "$e = 70^\\circ$: corresponding to $c$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "c and e are on the same side of the crossing line: co-interior.", "c and e are not in the same place at each crossing."] explain: "Co-interior angles add to 180°: e = 110°." ``` ### Triangle ### Quadrilateral ### Exterior angle backwards ### Review: parallel lines ## Make: a given exterior angle ```step stage: make insight: "Making a triangle with a given exterior angle reverses the reasoning: x = 135° needs c = 45°, from a + b = 135°." try: { playground: board, starter: "shapes.yml#make", height: 600 } hint: ["x = 135° means c = 45°.", "A right angle at A and equal legs give 45° at C: try A (1, 1), B (7, 1), C (1, 7)."] check: { type: board, text: "Move the corners so that the exterior angle $x$ is $135^\\circ$.", when: "x = 135", explain: "c = 45°, so a + b = 135°: for example a = 90° and b = 45°." } ``` First work out what $c$ must be. Then find a triangle that has it. Stretch: design an angle puzzle for a partner with two unknown angles, and write the model reasons. ## Make: a rafter cut, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A roof gives a right-angled triangle, so the cut angle at the ridge is the third angle: 180° − 90° − pitch, with a reason for each step." hint: ["Which angle in the triangle is the right angle?", "Angles in a triangle add to 180°."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A roof has a pitch of 25°. The rafter, the upright ridge post and half the span (flat) make a right-angled triangle. At what angle must the rafter be cut where it meets the ridge post? Give the angle in degrees." steps: - ["The post is upright and the span is flat, so they meet at $90^\\circ$", "a right-angled triangle"] - ["The pitch $25^\\circ$ is the angle at the bottom of the rafter", "given"] - ["Cut angle $= 180^\\circ - 90^\\circ - 25^\\circ = 65^\\circ$", "angles in a triangle add to $180^\\circ$"] - ["Check: $25 + 65 + 90 = 180$", "the three angles add to $180^\\circ$"] picks: - step: 3 q: "Why take 90° and 25° away from 180°?" options: - "Angles in a triangle add to 180°, and the post meets the span at 90°" - "The cut angle and the pitch add to 180°" - "The cut angle equals the pitch, because the rafter slopes both ways" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The pitch and the cut are two angles of one triangle, with the right angle too. Three angles add to 180°.", "The cut and the pitch are different angles of the triangle."] answer: "65" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["155", "That is 180° − 25°. The triangle also has a right angle, so take that away too."] - ["25", "That is the pitch. The cut angle is the third angle of the triangle."] criteria: - "I named the right angle and where it is." - "I gave a reason for the subtraction: angles in a triangle." - "I checked that 25 + 65 + 90 = 180." explain: "The triangle has angles 90°, 25° and the cut. 180° − 90° − 25° = 65°, so the rafter is cut at 65°." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The pitch is made up for the task, and a real roof has timber thickness to allow for. Sketch the triangle, mark the angles, write a reason for each line, then type the cut angle. **Also used in** - **Trusses and braces.** Builders work out the angle they cannot measure from the ones they can. - **Cutting timber.** An angled cut, such as a brace or a stair stringer, comes from the angles of a right-angled triangle. ```teacher summary: Students find unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals and pentagons in steps, with a reason for each (angle sum, straight line, isosceles), and explain why an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles; working is their own, the answer and a key reason are marked (AC9M7M05, node 3). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can find an unknown angle in a triangle or polygon using its angle sum. - I can combine angle sums with straight-line and parallel-line angles, giving a reason for each step. - I can explain why an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. struggle: Giving a reason for each step. Ask students to say which fact they used (angles in a triangle, a straight line, a right angle) before they write the number. before: > Do the first reasoning task yourself, then compare with its model. Students need Angles in a triangle, Angles in a polygon and Reasoning with angles. The one idea: choose the right angle sum for the shape, then chain steps with reasons. The common mistake is using 180° for every shape; it is planted in Zoe's working, where a negative angle is the clue. As in Reasoning with angles, the free working is not marked: students write it their way. The answer is marked, and at the key step they choose the reason from a list. Then they compare with a model and tick a self-check. The isosceles task is wider than the minimum: the equal angles are stated in the question. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands, then ask students who chose 110° how they got it. Collect both routes (two steps, or a + b)." - "Run: ask why x = a + b must be true (a + b + c = 180° and x + c = 180°)." - "Investigate: model know, choose, say why for the triangle. Ask: what does a negative answer tell you (Zoe)?" - "Modify: before the pentagon, ask students for its angle sum and how they know." - "Make: ask students what c must be before they move anything." - "Paper: the rafter task is worked in books; the page marks the cut angle (65) and the reason for the subtraction. Books out, then look at the page for the 180° check." stuck: - see: A student uses 180° for a quadrilateral (Zoe's mistake). ask: How many triangles does a quadrilateral split into? fix: "(n − 2) × 180°: two triangles, 360°." - see: A student stops at the interior angle when asked for the exterior one. ask: Which angle is x? Is it inside the triangle? fix: Mark x on the diagram, then find what links it to an angle you have (a straight line). - see: A student writes numbers with no reasons. ask: Which fact did you use for that line? fix: "One reason per line, in short words: 'angle sum of triangle', 'straight line'." stretch: Prove that the exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360°, starting from a triangle (each exterior + interior = 180°). support: "Use the Run board to check: set a triangle, read its angles, and compare with your working." leads: > This completes the Year 7 angle work: parallel lines (AC9M7M04) and angle sums (AC9M7M05). Where it leads: congruence and similarity (Years 8 and 9) and geometric proof, where chains of reasons are the whole point. exit: q: A triangle has angles of 48° and 67°. Find the third angle, and the exterior angle next to it, with reasons. a: "180° − 48° − 67° = 65° (angles in a triangle). Exterior angle 180° − 65° = 115° (a straight line). Check: 48° + 67° = 115°." explain: > To find an unknown angle in a shape, choose the **angle sum** for the shape: $180^\circ$ for a triangle, $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$ for $n$ sides ($360^\circ$ for a quadrilateral, $540^\circ$ for a pentagon). Add the angles you know and subtract from the sum. Combine it with other facts, one step at a time, each with a reason. Extend a side of a triangle and the outside angle $x$ makes a straight line with $c$: $x = 180^\circ - c$. Since $a + b = 180^\circ - c$ too, **$x = a + b$**. ```
